content: Intraperitoneal adhesions are a significant medical concern, as they are associated with various complications, including chronic pelvic pain, dyspareunia (painful intercourse), subfertility, and bowel obstruction. These adhesions also make subsequent surgeries more challenging, prolong operative times, and increase the risk of complications. The substantial burden of adhesions has driven the development of anti-adhesion agents, but there is ongoing debate regarding their relative effectiveness. The objective of this study was to evaluate the clinical safety and effectiveness of different types of anti-adhesion agents—solid, gel, liquid, and pharmacological—used as adjuncts to prevent adhesion formation following gynecological pelvic surgery. The evidence was derived from Cochrane systematic reviews. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews was searched up to August 2014 using the keyword adhesion. Additional searches were conducted in the Cochrane information management system for ongoing reviews. Two independent reviewers extracted data, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. The quality of the included reviews was assessed narratively and formally using the AMSTAR tool, while the quality of evidence in the original studies was evaluated using GRADE methods. Two Cochrane reviews were included in this analysis. The first review examined 18 studies comparing solid agents (oxidized regenerated cellulose, expanded polytetrafluoroethylene, sodium hyaluronate and carboxymethylcellulose, and fibrin sheets) with control or with each other. The second review included 29 studies comparing liquid agents (4% icodextrin, 32% dextran, crystalloids), gel agents (carboxymethylcellulose and polyethylene oxide, polyethylene glycol gels, hyaluronic acid-based gel, 0.5% ferric hyaluronate gel, sodium hyaluronate spray), and pharmacological agents (gonadotrophin-releasing hormone agonist, reteplase plasminogen activator, N,O-carboxymethyl chitosan, steroid agents, intraperitoneal noxytioline, intraperitoneal heparin, systemic promethazine) with control or with each other. Both reviews met all AMSTAR criteria. The reviews included both primary outcomes (pelvic pain, pregnancy, live birth rate, and quality of life) and secondary outcomes (adverse effects, presence or absence of adhesions at second-look laparoscopy, and adhesion scores). However, no primary studies of solid, gel, or pharmacological agents reported data on the primary outcomes. Only studies of liquid agents versus control (saline or Hartmann's solution) reported on primary outcomes, including pelvic pain (two studies), live birth (two studies), and pregnancy (three studies). Of the 47 studies included across both reviews, 25 reported external funding, with 24 of these funded by commercial sources. For solid agents, none of the primary outcomes were reported. Adverse events were reported in only 9 of the 18 studies, and no adverse events were noted in these reports. For liquid agents, there was no evidence of a difference between liquid agents and control (saline or Hartmann's solution) in terms of pelvic pain (odds ratio [OR] 0.65, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.37 to 1.14, 1 study, n = 286, moderate-quality evidence), pregnancy rate (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.14, 3 studies, n = 310, moderate-quality evidence), or live birth rate (OR 0.67, 95% CI 0.29 to 1.58, 2 studies, n = 208, moderate-quality evidence). None of the studies reported on quality of life, and adverse events were not reported as an outcome in any of the nine studies. For gel agents, none of the primary outcomes were reported, and adverse events were not reported in any of the seven studies. For pharmacological agents, none of the primary outcomes were reported. Adverse events were reported in only one of the seven studies. This study found no evidence of a difference in ectopic pregnancy rates between intraperitoneal noxytioline and no treatment (OR 4.91, 95% CI 0.45 to 53.27, 1 study, n = 33, low-quality evidence). In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness and safety of anti-adhesion agents in gynecological surgery. Data on critical outcomes such as pelvic pain, fertility outcomes, quality of life, and safety are lacking. A significant proportion of research in this field has been funded by private companies that manufacture these agents. High-quality, independent trials are needed to draw definitive conclusions.
